v.q: What must be true of the data before you can use binary search?
o: It must be sorted and allow random access
It must contain no duplicate values
It must be stored in a linked list
It must contain fewer than a thousand items
v.w: Halving the range relies on the order, and jumping to the middle in O(1) needs an array or ArrayList.
Binary search needs order and constant-time access to the middle element.

v.q: Why write mid as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 instead of (lo + hi) / 2?
o: The sum lo + hi can overflow an int on very large arrays
It makes the loop run twice as fast
It avoids sorting the array first
It is required for the array to have even length
v.w: For indexes near Integer.MAX_VALUE the sum wraps to a negative number. The subtraction form cannot overflow.

v.q: What is the risk in int mid = (lo + hi) / 2?
v.w: For very large indexes lo + hi exceeds the int range, so use lo + (hi - lo) / 2.

v.q: What does Arrays.binarySearch return when the key is missing?
o: The index of the largest smaller element
v.w: Any negative result means not found, and -result - 1 is the position where the key would be inserted to keep the array sorted.

v.q: Which value does Arrays.binarySearch return for a missing key that belongs at index 3?
v.w: It returns -(insertion point) - 1, so -4 tells you to insert at 3.

v.q: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be stable?
o: Equal elements keep their original relative order
It always runs in the same amount of time
v.w: Stability matters when sorting records by several keys in turn. Merge sort and TimSort are stable; quicksort and heap sort usually are not.
Merge sort keeps equal elements in their original order.

v.q: Why is merge sort O(n log n) in every case?
o: There are about log n levels of splitting and each level does O(n) merge work
It sorts each element with a single comparison
It only compares neighbouring elements once
It never needs to merge two sorted halves
v.w: The splits do not depend on the data, so the best, average and worst cases are the same.

v.q: Which statement about merge sort is NOT true?
o: It is O(n log n) in every case
v.w: The standard algorithm needs O(n) extra space for merging.

v.q: When does quicksort degrade to O(n²)?
o: When the pivot is repeatedly the smallest or largest element
When the array contains only distinct values
When the array has an even number of elements
When it is called recursively on both halves
v.w: Extreme pivots create very unbalanced splits, for example always taking the first element of already sorted data. Random or median-of-three pivots avoid it.

v.q: Which input makes a naive quicksort with the first element as pivot slow?
o: An array of distinct random values
v.w: The pivot is always the smallest, so the split is lopsided and the cost becomes O(n squared).

v.q: Which sort does Java use for List.sort and Arrays.sort on objects?
o: TimSort, a stable merge and insertion hybrid
A dual-pivot quicksort that is not stable at all
v.w: Primitive arrays use a dual-pivot quicksort; object sorts must be stable, so they use TimSort.

v.q: Which statement about Java sorting is NOT true?
o: Arrays.sort on objects is not stable
v.w: Sorting objects is stable, so equal elements keep their order.

v.q: You need the 10 largest values from a stream of millions. What is the better approach?
o: Keep a min-heap of size 10 and drop the smallest when it grows
Sort the whole stream and take the last 10
Store everything in a HashSet and scan it ten times
Use binary search on the unsorted stream
v.w: A heap of size k costs O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, and works on data that does not fit in memory.

v.q: Which structure finds the median of a stream most efficiently?
v.w: A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half give the median in O(1) and insertion in O(log n).
